interactions.summary: A student compares kissing Virgil’s feet to biblical worship, and Jiang rejects humility as the explanation for Virgil’s discomfort.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student proposal followed by Jiang correction.

interactions.summary: Jiang argues Virgil is disturbed because Statius is a pagan poet like himself yet somehow surpasses him, leading into a broader claim that people can never fully fool themselves.
Jiang invents an Ivy-at-Harvard thought experiment, and the class names jealousy as the human reaction Virgil is experiencing when a former admirer has gone farther than he did.

claims.claim: Jiang says Virgil is not acting humble before Statius; he is irritated because Statius should, by Virgil’s own pagan logic, not outrank him.
Jiang claims a person can never fully fool himself because some dimension of the self still knows the truth.
Jiang reads Virgil as knowing internally that pagans can reach heaven, even while refusing to admit it openly because face matters to him more than truth.
The Ivy analogy reframes Virgil’s reaction as recognizably human jealousy when a former student or admirer surpasses the master.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns Virgil into a case study in irreducible self-knowledge: you can fool the world but not yourself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's no way you can ever fool yourself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This becomes the engine of Virgil’s discomfort and Jiang’s broader psychology of bad faith.

signature_moments.moment: The Harvard student thought experiment compresses Virgil’s cosmic jealousy into a teacher watching a student outrun him.
signature_moments.source_phrase: oh i'm teaching dante at harvard
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The analogy makes the theological problem feel immediate and human-sized.

chronology_notes.note: This is a strong June 26 formulation of Jiang’s self-deception model: truth persists in the self even when the conscious story is evasive.
